title: Nominalization
definition: A derivational process that forms a noun stem from a verb (or other) root. Dixon (§11.3) notes that nominalization is cross-linguistically more common than verbalization, which correlates with the fact that verbs functioning as NP heads is rarer than nouns functioning as predicate heads — when something unusual happens in syntax, the language tends to have an explicit morphological strategy for it. Nominalizations can derive: the agent of an action (Tagalog *taga-sulat* 'writer' ← *sulat* 'write'), the instrument (Fijian *i-cula* 'needle' ← *cula* 'pierce'), the place (*i-moce-moce* 'bed' ← *moce* 'sleep'), or the activity itself as an abstract noun. Nominalizations differ from [term:zero-derivation] in that the derivation is morphologically marked. They also differ from simple NP-headedness (scheme III/IV), where the verb itself — without derivation — fills the NP slot.

examples.notes: Dixon (§11.3 Table 11.4): observe → observation (suffix -ion); also observe → observer (suffix -er). These are nominalizations with overt marking. The corresponding zero-derived pair would be 'concern' (verb) → 'concern' (noun, zero suffix).
Dixon (§11.8): Tagalog prefix taga- added to verb root creates an agentive noun 'the person employed to perform the action'. A morphologically explicit nominalization.
Dixon (§11.8): Fijian prefix i- derives instrument nouns from verb roots. Also: i-vola 'letter/book' ← vola 'write'; i-moce-moce 'bed' ← moce 'sleep' (with reduplication).
